UNIT 18: URBAN GROWTH AND SUSTAINABILITY

KEY THEME
- Urbanisation is the spread of towns and cities into the surrounding countryside to house a growing population. It brings challenges, so responses must be well planned and sustainable to protect quality of life and the natural environment.

KEY TERMS
- Urban place: a town or city with over 1,500 people (CSO definition).
- Urbanisation: the process where more people move to cities, increasing the urban population; the physical spread of urban centres into the countryside.
- Globalisation: the growing connection between countries through trade, travel, technology and culture.
- Gentrification: when a poorer urban area is improved and wealthier people move in, often raising rents and pushing out existing residents.
- Commuter: a person who regularly travels between home and work or school.
- Urban sprawl: the spread of a city into rural land in a low-density, unplanned, poorly managed way.
- Compact growth: building closer together to limit sprawl and use land efficiently.
- Rent pressure zones: areas where rent increases are limited by law to protect tenants.
- Urban fringe: the outer edge of a city where urban and rural areas meet.
- Suburbanisation: movement of people and businesses from the city centre to the suburbs.
- Counter-urbanisation: people moving from cities to rural areas or smaller towns.
- Overspill settlement: a town outside a larger city that expands to house people because of a housing shortage in the city.
- Zoning: deciding which types of development are allowed in different areas; rezoning is changing these land uses.
- Brownfield site: land previously used but now waste ground or derelict.
- Green belt / green space: areas where building is not permitted.
- Urban regeneration: improving run-down urban areas (renewal or redevelopment).
- Transport Orientated Development (TOD): planning housing, jobs and services around public transport hubs.
- Smart city: a city that uses technology and data to improve services, efficiency and quality of life.
- Ecocity: a city designed to be environmentally friendly, with renewable energy, green spaces and low pollution.

URBANISATION: FACTS AND FIGURES
- Over 55% of the world's population live in urban areas (UN); projected 68% by 2050.
- Ireland: most people lived in rural areas until 1971. Today almost 63% (3.3 million) are urban, expected to reach 75% by 2050.
- Ireland has 218 urban settlements, but 25% of the population (1.3 million) live in Dublin; this could rise to 40% by 2050.
- Projected growth 2022-2040 (table): Dublin city and suburbs 1,263,000, up 20-25% (296,000 people); Cork 223,000, up 40% (96,000); Limerick 102,000, up 40% (44,000); Galway 86,000, up 40% (36,000); Waterford 60,000, up 40% (28,000).

FACTORS INFLUENCING URBANISATION
- Migration and population growth are the biggest drivers. Other factors: globalisation, employment, services and planning strategies.
- Globalisation: connectivity, trade and capital create wealth and jobs in global cities. Dublin used its low corporation tax rate and educated workforce to attract foreign direct investment (FDI). Multinationals such as Google, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft have European headquarters in Dublin, making it a global city and a strong pull factor. International migrants also come (e.g. Ukrainians since 2022). 2022 Census: 17% of Dublin residents are 'non-Irish'.
- Employment: jobs concentrate in urban areas; rural-urban migration grew since the Industrial Revolution. Over half of Ireland's most populated towns are in the Greater Dublin and Greater Cork Areas, many as commuter or overspill towns (e.g. Navan, Co. Meath; Blarney, Co. Cork). Dublin's 'Silicon Docks' (Google, Facebook, Accenture, Airbnb, Indeed) gives high-paid jobs that attract young professionals; growth creates more service jobs, continuing the cycle.
- Services: transport (e.g. Luas), healthcare, education, retail and entertainment are pull factors, but rapid growth puts pressure on housing and transport.
- Planning strategies: zoning and rezoning manage land use. Without planning, growth causes sprawl, congestion and lower quality of life. Dublin City Development Plan 2022-2028: compact, higher-density housing in the centre and on brownfield sites; better public transport, walking and cycling; protecting green spaces.

IMPACTS OF URBANISATION IN DUBLIN
- Five impacts: urban sprawl and suburbanisation; pressure on services; gentrification, land values and rent pressure; urban decay; counter-urbanisation.

URBAN SPRAWL: CAUSES
- Dublin grew outwards in low-rise, low-density housing (not high-rise), reaching into Meath, Kildare, Wicklow and even Westmeath: the Greater Dublin Area (GDA). Satellite images from 1984 and 2022 show this low-density growth.
- Causes: rapid population growth since the early 1970s; poor inner-city housing led to farmland on the fringe being rezoned; cultural preference for owning single-family homes (the 'territorial imperative'); planning policies that favoured low-rise development near routeways; corrupt planning rezoned green belts between Tallaght, Lucan and Clondalkin, and developers sought profitable low-density rezoning; high prices and rents push people out; many local authorities (four Dublin councils plus Meath, Kildare and Wicklow) so planning is poorly coordinated; more car ownership and little investment in public transport; suburban hubs near motorways such as Liffey Valley.
- Geofact: John Speed's 1612 map 'Dubline' is the oldest surviving map of Dublin, with 69 placenames.

URBAN SPRAWL: IMPACTS
- Commuting and congestion: public transport is not keeping up in Meath, Kildare and Wicklow, so car use rises; chronic congestion on routes like the M50. Average Irish commute was 29.1 minutes in 2022 (double the EU average); many near Dublin commute over an hour - the 'one-hour city'. (Jakarta citizens spend over 400 hours a year in traffic.)
- Absence of community and wellbeing: less time and energy for clubs and charities; no sense of identity; social isolation; obesity risk; stress from traffic.
- Damage to the rural environment: fertile farmland in Meath and Kildare is lost to housing, factories and retail parks. Woodland, hedgerows and wetlands are destroyed, harming red squirrels, pine martens, hares, badgers and foxes, and pollinators lose food. More waste, pollution and car emissions. Urban foxes now scavenge bins and have shorter lives.

PRESSURE ON SERVICES AND INFRASTRUCTURE
- Housing crisis: acute shortage, soaring prices and rents, pushing people to the commuter belt (protests in Parnell Square, July 2025).
- Water: the GDA will need 34% more water by 2034; Uisce Eireann warns it lacks capacity without major upgrades.
- Electricity: EirGrid says population growth plus data centres have 'saturated' the network (e.g. Castlebaggot substation).

GENTRIFICATION, LAND VALUES AND RENT PRESSURE
- High-income residents move into lower-income areas, changing the social make-up. Example: Dublin Docklands, now a tech and finance hub.
- Brings new amenities but raises land prices and rents, pricing out long-standing families and 'hollowing out' communities.
- Example: Inchicore, Dublin 8 - a three-bed semi-detached house sold for over 500,000 euro in 2025.
- Short-term rentals like Airbnb reduce long-term homes.

URBAN DECAY
- An area showing social, economic and population decline: run-down, derelict buildings.
- Causes: businesses moved to cheaper greenfield suburban sites; poor planning and services; schools, shops and post offices close; those left are often older, poorer or less educated.
- Effects: loss of community spirit, alienation, anti-social behaviour (vandalism, drugs, crime). Speculators may leave buildings empty to rise in value. Examples: O'Connell Street Upper and Parnell Street.

COUNTER-URBANISATION
- Mature suburbs such as parts of Tallaght, Blanchardstown and Templeogue are losing population as residents age and children leave.
- Remote workers move to distant towns for better work-life balance. Example: Allenwood, Co. Kildare grew 494%, from 341 (1996) to 1,685 (2022), over 60 km from Dublin.
- Challenge: rural settlements may lack water, public transport, school places and healthcare.

SUSTAINABLE RESPONSES: NATIONAL PLANNING FRAMEWORK (PROJECT IRELAND 2040)
- Dublin is expected to grow by another 296,000 by 2040 (not counting Meath, Wicklow and Kildare).
- The NPF guides councils using National Strategic Outcomes based on the UN Sustainable Development Goals.
- Compact growth: higher-density housing on brownfield, derelict and vacant sites; target 50% of new homes in cities built this way by 2040.
- Integrated public transport (bus, rail, DART, Luas, taxis), walking and cycling. All new developments must be TODs. Example: Clonburris, South Dublin - population 23,000 when complete, 12 minutes from the city by rail (e.g. Seven Mills).
- Stronger regions: 'regional parity' (50:50 growth between the Eastern and Midland region and the other regions). Investment in Cork, Galway, Limerick and Waterford to attract FDI and become 'regional economic engines' (e.g. Dexcom near Athenry), slowing Dublin sprawl.
- Protecting green spaces: Tymon Park, Dodder Valley Park, Grand Canal.
- Tackling urban decay through urban regeneration.
- '15-minute city': everything within a 15-minute walk or cycle; promoted by the Eastern and Midland Regional Assembly (EMRA).

URBAN REGENERATION: RENEWAL VS REDEVELOPMENT
- Urban renewal: refurbish old buildings, replace derelict ones and add services (community centres, creches, parks, pitches). The function stays the same (usually residential) and people stay in their neighbourhood. Examples: Ballymun, Fatima Mansions, Clerys Quarter (Clerys closed 2015, reopened 2024; opened 1853 as the 'Palatial Mart', destroyed in the 1916 Rising, rebuilt 1922; famous Clerys Clock).
- Urban redevelopment: original residents rehoused elsewhere, old buildings demolished or repurposed, and the function changes (e.g. residential or industrial to commercial). Example: Dublin Docklands (old industrial and warehousing, now commercial, recreational and cultural). Also new building on brownfield or under-used greenfield sites like Clonburris.

CASE STUDY: URBAN REDEVELOPMENT - SMITHFIELD
- North inner city; Irish name Margadh na Feirme ('Farm Market'); livestock market from the 17th century, horse fairs and produce markets. Severe decay in the 20th century.
- 1995: Dublin City Council's Historic Area Rejuvenation Plan/Project (HARP) kept historic character while adding modern features. Smithfield Plaza: cobblestones lifted, cleaned and re-laid; twelve 26.5 m gas lighting masts.
- New apartments and offices; former Jameson Distillery became a visitor centre; Lighthouse Cinema; Luas line improved connectivity.
- Criticism: gentrification raised prices, pricing out long-term residents; does not meet needs of vulnerable groups. Overall seen as a successful template.

CASE STUDY: URBAN RENEWAL - BALLYMUN
- Built 1966-1969 to ease a housing crisis: seven 15-storey towers plus lower blocks, over 3,000 dwellings.
- Problems: poor quality, damp, cold, lifts rarely worked; no shops, pitches, playgrounds, creches or community centre; understaffed healthcare; high unemployment; isolation, alienation, anti-social behaviour; known for decay by the 1970s.
- 1997: government approved renewal; Ballymun Regeneration Limited (BRL) set up; cost about 972 million euro up to 2026.
- Physical renewal: towers demolished 2004-2015; new low-rise, high-density, mixed-tenure housing (private, social, affordable); new main street, parks, Ballymun Civic Centre, Axis Arts Centre.
- Economic renewal: IKEA opened its first Irish store in 2009 (about 730 jobs); hotel and retail units, but the 2008 financial crisis left sites vacant (planned shopping centre, cinema and bowling alley did not happen).
- Social renewal: education, health and community programmes, e.g. Ballymun Local Drugs Task Force and Slaintecare Healthy Communities.
- Criticism: over budget, behind schedule, incomplete due to reliance on private investment; deep social and economic inequality not fully solved.

DUBLIN AS A SMART CITY
- Smart city: digital technology and data built into services (health, transport, education, crime prevention); sensors collect data on energy use, waste and hospital waits to support better decisions.
- Smart Dublin (2016): the four Dublin councils (Dublin City, Fingal, South Dublin, Dun Laoghaire-Rathdown) with tech firms (e.g. Google), universities (Trinity, DCU) and citizens. Focus: climate change, sustainability, communication with citizens, congestion and mobility, better decisions and services, community engagement, physical and mental health.
- Smart Docklands (2018) is one of five areas (with Balbriggan, DCU, Dublin 8, Dun Laoghaire) using the Internet of Things (IoT).
- Docklands GIS avatar: 3D virtual model to test projects (e.g. new developments, disability access) before building.
- Big Belly Smart Bins: 110 bins holding up to five times more waste; solar-powered compactor every hour; sensors report fill levels to the council.
- Dublin on Water: 14 sensors on the Liffey give real-time level and flow data on the Smart Dublin App for boaters, walkers, emergency services and planners.
- Geofact: Singapore (5.9 million people) is the world's smartest city; Smart Nation Initiative 2014 cost S$2.4 billion; nationwide fibre network, 150% mobile coverage, 88% of households online.

DUBLIN AS AN ECOCITY
- An ecocity adds green spaces, improves biodiversity and air quality, uses renewable energy and reduces waste and pollution.
- Project Air View (2021): Dublin City Council, Google and Aclima used Google's first electric Street View car with Aclima sensors for 16 months; over 50 million measurements at 5 million locations, over 30,000 km. 2023 data showed six pollutants (CO2, CO, ozone, NO, NO2, PM2.5) with high NO along the quays from traffic.
- Parks Services: more trees, green or wildlife corridors, green infrastructure (green roofs, parks, rain gardens), no pesticides.
- Bridgefoot Street Park, the Liberties (2022, designed by DFLA): built with reused materials; over 180 trees planted; plants store carbon, reduce run-off and boost biodiversity.

rows.prompt: What is urbanisation?
options: The physical spread of towns and cities into the countryside
The movement of people from cities to rural villages
The building of new farms on the edge of towns
The closure of shops and services in town centres
rows.explanation: Urbanisation is urban growth: the spread of towns and cities into the surrounding countryside.

rows.prompt: What share of the world's population is projected to live in urban areas by 2050?
rows.explanation: The UN estimates over 55% now, projected to reach 68% by 2050.

rows.prompt: Until which year did most people in Ireland live in rural areas?
rows.explanation: The majority of Ireland's population lived in rural areas up until 1971.

rows.prompt: What share of Ireland's population lives in Dublin?
options: About 10%
About 40%
About 63%
About 25%
rows.explanation: About 25% (1.3 million) live in Dublin; this could rise to 40% by 2050.

rows.prompt: How did Dublin attract foreign direct investment?
options: High grants for farming
A large supply of cheap land
A national ban on imported goods
Low corporation tax and an educated workforce
rows.explanation: Dublin used its low corporation tax rate and educated workforce to attract FDI.

rows.prompt: What is an overspill settlement?
options: A part of a city built on reclaimed land from the sea
A town outside a city that grows to house people the city cannot
An area of a city that floods regularly
A suburb with more jobs than houses
rows.explanation: An overspill settlement expands to house people because of a housing shortage in the larger city.

rows.prompt: Which is an example of a commuter town for Cork?
options: Navan
Bray
Blarney
Allenwood
rows.explanation: The chapter names Blarney in Co. Cork and Navan in Co. Meath as commuter settlements.

rows.prompt: What does 'rezoning' mean?
options: Changing the land use allowed in an area
Building taller houses in a city
Moving a council to a new building
Dividing a city into new postcodes
rows.explanation: Zoning sets land uses in areas; rezoning changes them to other uses.

rows.prompt: How has Dublin mainly grown?
options: Outwards in low-density housing
Upwards in high-rise towers
Inwards by filling city-centre gaps
Onto land reclaimed from Dublin Bay
rows.explanation: Dublin has expanded outwards in low-rise, low-density settlement into Meath, Kildare and Wicklow.

rows.prompt: What is the 'territorial imperative'?
options: A law that protects green belts
A rule limiting the height of buildings
The preference for owning a single-family home
The right of councils to rezone land
rows.explanation: There is a cultural preference for single-family homes and owning them, the 'territorial imperative'.

rows.prompt: Why has planning across the Greater Dublin Area been poorly coordinated?
options: One national body controls all planning decisions
Several separate local authorities share the area
Planning laws do not apply to commuter towns
The EU makes all zoning decisions for Dublin
rows.explanation: The GDA has four Dublin councils plus Meath, Kildare and Wicklow councils, leading to a lack of coordination.

rows.prompt: What was the average commute in Ireland in 2022?
options: 15.2 minutes
45 minutes
60 minutes
29.1 minutes
rows.explanation: The CSO average was 29.1 minutes, double the EU average.

rows.prompt: Why is Dublin called the 'one-hour city'?
options: Its centre can be crossed in an hour
Its trains run once an hour
Its shops close one hour early
Many commuters take over an hour to reach work
rows.explanation: Many people in counties bordering Dublin take over an hour to get to work.

rows.prompt: Which is an impact of urban sprawl on the rural environment?
options: More hedgerows planted around estates
Loss of fertile farmland and habitats
Cleaner rivers near new housing
Higher numbers of red squirrels
rows.explanation: Sprawl uses fertile land in Meath and Kildare and destroys woodland, hedgerows and wetlands.

rows.prompt: How much more water will the GDA need by 2034?
rows.explanation: The GDA will need 34% more water by 2034, according to Uisce Eireann.

rows.prompt: Why does EirGrid say Dublin's electricity network is 'saturated'?
options: Population growth and many data centres
Old power stations closing down
Storms damaging power lines
Too many solar panels on roofs
rows.explanation: An increasing population plus the large number of data centres has saturated the network.

rows.prompt: What is gentrification?
options: Wealthier people moving into a poorer area, raising prices
Older people leaving the suburbs for the countryside
Businesses moving to greenfield sites in the suburbs
Councils demolishing high-rise flats
rows.explanation: Gentrification is when high-income residents move into a lower-income area, raising rents and pushing out residents.

rows.prompt: Which Dublin area is a prime example of gentrification?
options: Ballymun
Allenwood
The Docklands
Tallaght
rows.explanation: The redeveloped Dublin Docklands is a hub for tech and finance and a prime example.

rows.prompt: Why did urban decay happen in parts of inner-city Dublin?
options: New Luas lines brought too many visitors
Businesses moved to cheaper greenfield sites in the suburbs
Rent pressure zones lowered property values
Green spaces replaced shops and offices
rows.explanation: Local businesses and industries closed and moved to cheaper suburban greenfield sites.

rows.prompt: By how much did Allenwood, Co. Kildare grow between 1996 and 2022?
rows.explanation: Allenwood grew 494%, from 341 to 1,685 people.

rows.prompt: What is a challenge caused by counter-urbanisation?
options: City centres become too crowded with workers
Farmland prices fall sharply in rural areas
Suburbs become filled with young families
Rural towns may lack water, schools and transport
rows.explanation: Growing rural settlements may not have the infrastructure to support more people.

rows.prompt: What is the NPF target for new homes on brownfield and infill sites in cities by 2040?
rows.explanation: The target is that 50% of all new homes in Dublin and other cities are built this way by 2040.

rows.prompt: What is a Transport Orientated Development?
options: A motorway built around the edge of a city
A car park built next to a shopping centre
Housing and jobs planned around public transport hubs
A train depot for repairing carriages
rows.explanation: TOD plans housing, jobs and services around public transport to reduce reliance on cars.

rows.prompt: What does 'regional parity' mean in the NPF?
options: A 50:50 split of growth between Eastern-Midland and other regions
Equal rents in every region
Equal numbers of councils in each county
Equal public transport fares across Ireland
rows.explanation: Regional parity is a 50:50 distribution of growth between the Eastern and Midland region and the other regions.

rows.prompt: What is the '15-minute city'?
options: Everything needed is within 15 minutes' walk or cycle
Every bus arrives within 15 minutes
Commutes are limited to 15 minutes by law
Shops open for 15 hours a day
rows.explanation: Residents can reach almost everything they need within a quarter of an hour's walk or cycle.

rows.prompt: What is the main difference between urban renewal and urban redevelopment?
options: Renewal changes the area's function; redevelopment keeps it
Renewal is private; redevelopment is always public
Renewal keeps the function; redevelopment changes it
Renewal happens in towns; redevelopment only in villages
rows.explanation: In renewal the original function stays the same; in redevelopment it changes, e.g. residential to commercial.

rows.prompt: What did HARP introduce in Smithfield Plaza?
options: A new shopping centre and cinema
Twelve tall gas lighting masts
Fifteen-storey apartment towers
A motorway link to the M50
rows.explanation: Twelve 26.5 m gas lighting masts were introduced and the cobblestones re-laid.

rows.prompt: Which company opened its first Irish store in Ballymun in 2009?
options: Google
Dexcom
Clerys
IKEA
rows.explanation: IKEA opened in Ballymun in 2009, creating about 730 jobs.

rows.prompt: Why was Ballymun's renewal left incomplete?
options: Residents refused to leave the towers
The towers were listed as heritage buildings
The EU withdrew its regeneration funding
Private investment faltered after the 2008 crisis
rows.explanation: The 2008 global financial crisis hit private investment, leaving key sites vacant.

rows.prompt: What does the Big Belly Smart Bin do?
options: Sorts recycling by colour
Compacts waste using solar power and reports fill levels
Turns food waste into compost overnight
Charges a fee each time it is used
rows.explanation: A solar-powered compactor squeezes waste hourly and a sensor reports capacity to the council.

rows.prompt: What did Project Air View find along Dublin's quays?
options: Very low levels of all pollutants
High levels of pollen from trees
High levels of nitric oxide from traffic
High levels of salt from the sea
rows.explanation: It showed elevated NO along the quays due to traffic congestion.

rows.prompt: Explain how globalisation has caused Dublin to grow.
rows.model_answer: Dublin used its low corporation tax and educated workforce to attract foreign direct investment. Multinationals like Google, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft set up European headquarters there, making it a global city. The jobs and wealth are a strong pull factor for migrants from Ireland and abroad.

rows.prompt: Give four causes of urban sprawl in Dublin.
rows.model_answer: Dublin's population has grown rapidly since the 1970s. There is a cultural preference for owning single-family homes, and planning favoured low-rise, low-density housing. Green belts were rezoned, sometimes through corrupt practices. High prices push people outwards and car ownership rose while public transport investment lagged.

rows.prompt: Describe how long commutes affect community and wellbeing.
rows.model_answer: People who commute long distances spend less time in their area and have less energy for clubs or charities. They may not know neighbours and feel socially isolated. Long drives raise the risk of obesity and traffic causes stress.

rows.prompt: Explain how gentrification can 'hollow out' traditional communities.
rows.model_answer: When wealthier people move into a lower-income area such as the Docklands, land prices and rents rise. Families who lived there for generations are priced out and move to the suburbs. The area's unique character and social fabric are replaced by new, wealthier arrivals.

rows.prompt: What is urban decay and what problems does it cause?
rows.model_answer: Urban decay is when an area shows social, economic and population decline, with run-down and derelict buildings. Services close and those left are often older or poorer. It can cause loss of community spirit, alienation and anti-social behaviour such as vandalism and crime, as seen on Parnell Street.

rows.prompt: Name three strategies of the National Planning Framework to manage urban growth.
rows.model_answer: The NPF promotes compact growth with higher-density housing on brownfield sites. It improves integrated public transport and requires Transport Orientated Development, as at Clonburris. It aims for regional parity by developing Cork, Galway, Limerick and Waterford as regional economic engines, and protects green spaces.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between urban renewal and urban redevelopment, with an example of each.
rows.model_answer: In urban renewal, buildings are refurbished or replaced and services added, but the function stays the same, so residents stay; Ballymun is an example. In urban redevelopment, residents are rehoused elsewhere and the function changes, for example from industrial to commercial; Smithfield and the Docklands are examples.

rows.prompt: Describe two Smart Docklands projects.
rows.model_answer: Big Belly Smart Bins compact waste with solar power and send fill levels to the council, so 110 bins hold up to five times more. Dublin on Water uses 14 sensors on the Liffey to give real-time river level and flow data on the Smart Dublin App. The Docklands GIS avatar lets planners test projects in 3D first.

rows.prompt: Describe two ways Dublin is trying to become an ecocity.
rows.model_answer: Project Air View measured air pollution street by street using Google's electric Street View car, showing high nitric oxide on the quays so the council can plan to cut emissions. Bridgefoot Street Park in the Liberties was built from reused materials with over 180 trees, which store carbon, reduce run-off and improve biodiversity.

rows.prompt: Examine the causes and impacts of urban sprawl in an Irish city you have studied. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: Dublin has grown outwards in low-rise, low-density housing into Meath, Kildare, Wicklow and Westmeath, forming the Greater Dublin Area. Its population has grown rapidly since the 1970s. Poor inner-city housing led to fringe farmland being rezoned, and there is a cultural preference for owning single-family homes. Planning favoured low-rise housing near routeways, while corrupt rezoning built on green belts between Tallaght, Lucan and Clondalkin. High prices push people further out, and with seven councils planning is uncoordinated. Car ownership rose while public transport lagged, and suburban hubs like Liffey Valley encouraged more sprawl. The impacts are serious. Commuting has caused congestion on the M50; the average commute in 2022 was 29.1 minutes, double the EU average, and many take over an hour, making Dublin the 'one-hour city'. Commuters have less time for community activities, feel isolated and suffer stress. Fertile farmland in Meath and Kildare is lost, and woodland, hedgerows and wetlands are destroyed, harming red squirrels, badgers and pollinators. More cars bring more emissions.

rows.prompt: Examine the impacts of urban redevelopment in a named Irish city you have studied. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: In Dublin, Smithfield in the north inner city was a livestock market from the 17th century, but suffered severe urban decay in the 20th century with derelict buildings and a declining population. In 1995 Dublin City Council's Historic Area Rejuvenation Plan (HARP) aimed to modernise it while keeping its character. Smithfield Plaza was redeveloped: cobblestones were lifted, cleaned and re-laid and twelve 26.5 m gas lighting masts created a striking public space that attracted businesses and residents. New apartments and offices brought new residents and companies. The former Jameson Distillery became a visitor centre and the Lighthouse Cinema opened, attracting tourists and spending. The Luas line linked Smithfield to the wider city, making it attractive to live and work in. However, gentrification has been a key problem. Wealthier residents have pushed up property and rental prices, pricing out long-term residents, and critics argue the needs of vulnerable groups in the north inner city were not met. Despite this, Smithfield is seen as a successful template, turning a decaying area into a vibrant, culturally rich neighbourhood.
rows.marking_scheme: Named city and area 2m (e.g. Dublin, Smithfield). Examination of impacts: 14 SRPs x 2m. Positive and/or negative impacts accepted; brief background max 2 SRPs. Max 30 marks.

rows.prompt: Describe and explain how urban growth is putting pressure on services and infrastructure in Dublin. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Dublin's rapid growth has outstripped its ability to provide housing, transport, water, electricity and waste services. The Greater Dublin Area has a housing crisis, an acute shortage of homes that has caused soaring prices and rents, leading to protests such as in Parnell Square in July 2025. Many are forced into the commuter belt, adding to sprawl. Short-term rentals like Airbnb further reduce homes available. Water supply is a major issue, as the GDA will need 34% more water by 2034 and Uisce Eireann warns it may not be able to connect new developments without upgrades. EirGrid says population growth and the many data centres have saturated the electricity network, for example at the Castlebaggot substation.
rows.marking_scheme: 10 SRPs x 2m. Credit named services, statistics and named organisations (Uisce Eireann, EirGrid) as SRPs. Max 20 marks.

rows.prompt: Discuss how Dublin is using smart city and ecocity strategies to respond to the challenges of urban growth. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: A smart city integrates digital technology and data into services so authorities can plan better. Dublin's four councils launched Smart Dublin in 2016 with Google, Trinity, DCU and citizens to tackle climate change, congestion, health and communication. Smart Docklands, launched in 2018, uses the Internet of Things. Its GIS avatar is a 3D virtual Docklands where planners test new developments and disability access before building. 110 Big Belly Smart Bins hold up to five times more waste, compacting it hourly with solar power and reporting fill levels, making collection efficient. Dublin on Water uses 14 Liffey sensors to give real-time level and flow data to boaters, walkers and emergency services. An ecocity adds green space, improves air quality and cuts its carbon footprint. Project Air View (2021) used Google's electric Street View car with Aclima sensors to collect over 50 million readings, finding high nitric oxide on the quays from traffic, which helps plan emission cuts. Parks Services are planting trees, creating wildlife corridors and green roofs and stopping pesticides. Bridgefoot Street Park (2022) was built from reused materials with over 180 trees that store carbon and reduce run-off.

rows.prompt: Explain three factors that have influenced the growth of urban areas in Ireland. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Globalisation: Dublin's low corporation tax and educated workforce attracted FDI, and multinationals like Google, Meta and Microsoft set up European headquarters, making it a global city that draws migrants; 17% of Dublin residents were non-Irish in 2022. Employment: jobs concentrate in cities, and Silicon Docks offers high-paid work that attracts young professionals, while growth creates more service jobs. Commuter towns such as Navan and Blarney grew as overspill settlements. Services: good transport like the Luas, healthcare, education and entertainment are pull factors that raise living standards. Planning strategies such as zoning and the Dublin City Development Plan 2022-2028 shape where growth happens.
rows.marking_scheme: Three factors named 2m each (6m). 7 SRPs x 2m spread across the factors. Max 20 marks.
